In summary, our research is concerned with
how climate and weather affect the biota of the Southern Ocean and the extent to which these effects can be detected and quantified.
the long-term changes in the climate of the Southern Ocean and their consequences for marine biota, and with the role of sea ice in mediating those consequences.
the effects of decadal-scale climate changes on the biota of the Southern Ocean and how these changes are manifested in population trends of ice-dependent species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
climate changes have affected Southern Ocean biota in a manner consistent with the effects of climate changes elsewhere.
, in the Southern Ocean, the 1970s and 1988–9 shifts in weather patterns, sea ice, polynyas and the biota were related.
, in the Pacific Sector at least, the two species' population trajectories were affected by a combination of changes in the strength of the semi-annual oscillation and the Antarctic oscillation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the two species' population shifts in both the 1970s and the 1980s were related to changes in the climate system of the Southern Ocean and that the shifts were widespread.
the Southern Ocean has experienced a series of decadal-scale climate shifts, which have affected the distribution and abundance of its ice-dependent biota.
the climate and biotic patterns of the Pacific sector were dominated by the semi-annual oscillation during the 1950–80 period, but were dominated by the Antarctic oscillation from the 1980s to 1990s.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the face of global warming, the Southern Ocean is responding in a highly variable way that may not be easily predicted from simple models based on the mean state of the climate.
, despite the large-scale nature of these changes, they were not necessarily uniform in their effects across the entire Southern Ocean.
the Southern Ocean is not a static environment.
